p.src: Overview: A magnetic field is divergence-free, so it can be represented by a vector potential. That representation is not unique, yet it is precisely what allows magnetic forces to enter the action principle. We derive the Lorentz force, distinguish canonical from mechanical momentum, construct the Hamiltonian, and use two different gauges to solve the motion in a uniform magnetic field. The lecture closes by locating this particle mechanics inside the larger subjects of Maxwell theory, magnetic monopoles, and phase-space dynamics.

ja: 概観: 磁場は発散がゼロであるため、ベクトルポテンシャルによって表すことができる。その表現は一意的ではないが、まさにそれによって磁気的な力を作用原理に取り入れることが可能になる。我々はローレンツ力を導出し、正準運動量と力学的運動量を区別し、ハミルトニアンを構成し、2つの異なるゲージを用いて一様磁場中の運動を解く。講義の最後には、この粒子力学がマクスウェル理論、磁気単極子、位相空間の力学というより大きな主題の中にどのように位置づけられるかを示す。
zh: 概述: 磁场是无散度的，因此可以用矢量势来表示。这种表示并不唯一，但正是这一点使得磁力能够进入作用量原理。我们推导洛伦兹力，区分正则动量与机械动量，构造哈密顿量，并用两种不同的规范求解均匀磁场中的运动。本讲最后将这种粒子力学置于麦克斯韦理论、磁单极子和相空间动力学这些更大的主题之中。

  =

  =B.$

u.src: Why a gauge shift does not change the trajectory

ja: ゲージシフトが軌道を変えない理由

p.src:
Before varying the action, let us check what a gauge transformation does to it. For fixed initial and final spacetime points, $\mathcal S[\mathbf x]
  =
  \int_{t_i}^{t_f}L\,dt.$ Under $\mathbf A\mapsto\mathbf A+\nabla S$, the change is $\begin{aligned}\Delta\mathcal S
  &=
  \frac{e}{c}
  \int_{t_i}^{t_f}
  \nabla S(\mathbf x)\cdot\dot{\mathbf x}\,dt\\
  &=
  \frac{e}{c}
  \int_{t_i}^{t_f}\frac{dS(\mathbf x(t))}{dt}\,dt\\
  &=
  \frac{e}{c}
  \left[
    S(\mathbf x_f)-S(\mathbf x_i)
  \right].\end{aligned}$ The numerical value of the action therefore changes. But the added term depends only on the fixed endpoints, not on the varied interior of the path. It has zero variation and cannot alter the stationary trajectory.

The Euler–Lagrange equations may be written $\dot p_i=\frac{\partial L}{\partial x_i},
  \qquad
  p_i=\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot x_i}.$ At this point we must distinguish two momenta. The familiar mechanical momentum is $\boldsymbol{\pi}=m\mathbf v.$ The canonical momentum is defined by the Lagrangian: $p_i
  =

  =
  \mathbf p-\frac{e}{c}\mathbf A
  =
  m\mathbf v
  }.$ For a free particle, or for an ordinary position-dependent potential, canonical and mechanical momentum agree. The magnetic interaction depends on velocity, so they no longer do.

The lecture works through one component slowly. For $p_x$, $p_x=m\dot x+\frac{e}{c}A_x(\mathbf x).$ Even though the external field is static, $A_x(\mathbf x(t))$ changes as the particle moves. Its total time derivative is $\frac{dA_x}{dt}
  =
  \frac{\partial A_x}{\partial x}\dot x
  +
  \frac{\partial A_x}{\partial y}\dot y
  +
  \frac{\partial A_x}{\partial z}\dot z.$ Consequently, $\dot p_x
  =
  m\ddot x
  +
  \frac{e}{c}
  \left(
    \partial_xA_x\,\dot x
    +
    \partial_yA_x\,\dot y
    +
    \partial_zA_x\,\dot z
  \right).$ The right side of the Euler–Lagrange equation is $\frac{\partial L}{\partial x}
  =
  \frac{e}{c}
  \left(
    \partial_xA_x\,\dot x
    +
    \partial_xA_y\,\dot y
    +
    \partial_xA_z\,\dot z
  \right).$ The terms $\partial_xA_x\,\dot x$ cancel. Grouping what remains by velocity component gives $\begin{aligned}m\ddot x
  &=
  \frac{e}{c}
  \left[
    \left(\partial_xA_y-\partial_yA_x\right)\dot y
    +
    \left(\partial_xA_z-\partial_zA_x\right)\dot z
  \right].\end{aligned}$

The next question is whether the same system has a Hamiltonian description. Begin with $\begin{aligned}p_x&=m\dot x+\frac{e}{c}A_x,\\
  p_y&=m\dot y+\frac{e}{c}A_y,\\
  p_z&=m\dot z+\frac{e}{c}A_z.\end{aligned}$ These relations can be inverted: $\begin{aligned}\dot x&=\frac{1}{m}\left(p_x-\frac{e}{c}A_x\right),\\

  H(\mathbf x,\mathbf p)
  =
  \frac{1}{2m}
  \left(
    \mathbf p-\frac{e}{c}\mathbf A(\mathbf x)
  \right)^2
  }.$

One final audience question asks about Hamilton’s quaternions. They are historically separate from Hamiltonian mechanics. Hamilton sought an algebra that could play for three-dimensional rotations something like the role complex numbers play for planar rotations. In quantum mechanics the same algebraic structure can be represented with Pauli matrices, with suitable factors of the ordinary imaginary unit. This connection is real, but it is not the origin of the canonical momentum or Hamiltonian developed in this course.
